title: The Maple Residences: extra-large spaces at a price below Bukit Jalil.
videoTitle: PROPERTY REVIEW #475 | THE MAPLE RESIDENCES, TAMAN OUG
excerpt: The second phase of a township between the KESAS and MEX highways, with hotel-like common areas, 3.4 m ceilings and lift lobbies split for privacy, priced well below Bukit Jalil across the road.
takeaways: Two lift lobbies per floor, split front and back, so fewer residents share each lift.
A 958 sq ft three-bedroom sells for about RM700,000 and rents for about RM4,000 furnished.
Highway noise when the windows are open, and generous common areas that will cost more to maintain.

sections.heading: What sets it apart
paragraphs: The Maple Residences is three towers, each with its own roundabout drop-off around a water feature, and a ground-floor multi-purpose hall so guests never need to go up to the residential floors. Every floor has two lift lobbies with three lifts each for 10 units, and a partition separates the front and back halves, so residents only meet the people on their own side.

Sean viewed a 958 sq ft three-bedroom, two-bathroom unit with a 3.4 m ceiling, a 3.3 m-wide living area and every bedroom on the facade; the master bedroom is 3.26 by 5.12 m. It has no balcony, because that side faces the highway.

sections.heading: Where it is
paragraphs: The project sits in Taman OUG at the junction of the KESAS and MEX highways, across KESAS from Bukit Jalil, next to IMU and Columbia Hospital, with Sri Petaling LRT station on the other side of the highway. It is the second phase of the developer's township after Waltz Residence, surrounded by established landed homes, schools and a row of shops nearby.

sections.heading: Rent and returns
paragraphs: Sean reads about RM700,000 for this unit on a listings site, about RM730 psf, and about RM620 psf for the 1,300 sq ft four-bedroom units, against about RM900 to RM1,000 psf for Bukit Jalil opposite. A fully furnished 958 sq ft unit rents for about RM4,000 a month and the smallest, 800 sq ft units for about RM3,000.
Tenants range from students and families to people working in central KL, and some owners let room by room. Some units were still unsold, so buyers can view the exact unit before committing.

standout.title: Lifts split by wing, not by floor
standout.body: Instead of splitting lifts into low and high floors, each floor has two lift lobbies, one for the front half and one for the back, chosen from the car park onwards. A partition between the halves means fewer residents share each lift and corridor, and there is even a separate lift lobby for visitors.

pros: The location: KESAS, MEX, MRR2, the North-South and KL-Seremban highways, Puchong, Kuchai Lama and Old Klang Road are all close, and as an old address it is surrounded by schools, universities and mature neighbourhoods. The LRT is across the highway rather than connected, which Sean, who avoids living by a station, doesn't mind.

The architecture: a drop-off for each tower, lift lobbies split front and back for privacy, wide corridors, 3.3 to 3.4 m ceilings and rooms about 10 to 15% larger than usual, which Sean calls this developer's signature. He loves the facilities, especially three floating pavilions for reading, yoga and games, and the car parks tucked into the drop from road to highway so the towers needn't be tall.
It is part of a master plan, so the roads, landscaping, walkways, drains and street lights are built from scratch, and the developer plans later phases with earlier buyers in mind.
cons: The micro setting: it sits between two highways, and with a window open you hear the traffic, though it goes quiet once closed and the pools at the front help mask it. The entrance runs under a highway link, and until the master plan opens another exit, the single left-turn access will be congested at peak hours.

Everything is bigger than it needs to be: three drop-offs, many lifts, several pools and 3.4 m ceilings all add to construction and maintenance costs, and water features are often the first thing to go once the joint management body takes over. He would also have liked room for a shoe cabinet and the washer and dryer built into the kitchen rather than standing in the middle of the home.

Competition: later phases of the township, a new launch beside the golf course, four or five towers in Bukit Jalil and a steady pipeline in Old Klang Road, Kuchai Lama and Taman Desa. Even so, rents of about RM4,000 and a wide pool of tenants show the demand.

closing: A project that exceeded Sean's expectations, for buyers who want generous space and privacy at a lower price than Bukit Jalil and can live with the highway outside.
sourceNote: Based on Sean's full English captions for this October 2026 episode and its video description. The 3 on 3 follows the three things he likes and the three he doesn't, in his order, at the end of the video. An owner let Sean view a furnished investment unit; prices and rents are as he quoted them. Sean mentions that he owns a unit in Johor Bahru built by the same developer.
